heuristics.rule: Ask to speak with a PhD student in year 4 or 5 in that specific lab, not a general program ambassador
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a PhD advisor or program before accepting an offer...
heuristics.action: ...specifically request contact with year 4-5 students in that advisor's lab, not first-year students or program-selected contacts
heuristics.because: Year 4-5 students are in the most vulnerable period — funding is ending, dissertation may be stalling — and their experience is the most predictive of what you will actually face

heuristics.rule: Treat any program with a 10-year completion rate below 60% as a red flag requiring explanation
heuristics.condition: When comparing PhD program offers and completion rate data is available...
heuristics.action: ...request the program's 10-year completion rate and apply a 60% floor as a minimum threshold before proceeding
heuristics.because: CGS data shows 25-43% of PhD students never finish; a below-60% rate indicates structural problems in funding, mentorship, or program design, not just individual student failure

heuristics.rule: Assume a 2-3 year funding gap between what is promised and when you will actually finish
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a PhD funding package that guarantees 4-5 years of support...
heuristics.action: ...plan financially for 6-7 years minimum and ask explicitly what happens to students after funded years end
heuristics.because: National median time to degree is 7.3 years; most funding guarantees only 4-5 years; the gap is where attrition and financial crises concentrate

heuristics.rule: A strong publication record in a faculty member does not predict good advising
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a potential PhD advisor based on their CV or lab prestige...
heuristics.action: ...treat publication record as orthogonal to mentorship quality and separately investigate mentorship behaviors through student conversations
heuristics.because: National Academies finding: mentorship is a learned skill, not a personality trait; negative mentorship patterns (credit-taking, absence, exploitation) are invisible in a publication list

heuristics.rule: Build a mentorship committee of at least 3 people before the end of your first year
heuristics.condition: When starting a PhD program with a single assigned advisor...
heuristics.action: ...proactively cultivate co-advisors, engaged thesis committee members, and peer mentors in senior years rather than waiting for the program to structure this
heuristics.because: Single-advisor models create a single point of failure; National Academies data shows multiple mentoring relationships improve completion and career outcomes

heuristics.rule: Ask for the advisor-specific time-to-degree, not the program average
heuristics.condition: When evaluating time-to-completion expectations for a PhD program...
heuristics.action: ...ask 'what is the average time to degree for students who have graduated from this specific lab in the last 5 years' rather than accepting department-level statistics
heuristics.because: Advisor-specific time-to-degree varies enormously within the same program; department averages obscure individual advisor patterns that directly predict your experience

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Advisor relationship problems are the most commonly cited reason for leaving a PhD program; mentorship quality predicts both completion and long-term career outcomes
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Talk to current year 4-5 students and recent graduates specifically; ask whether the advisor provides both career support (technical guidance, networking) AND psychosocial support (encouragement, validation); ask about meeting frequency and whether the advisor was available during difficult periods

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Funding interruptions are a primary predictor of attrition; the gap between guaranteed funding (4-5 years) and actual completion time (7+ years) creates a structural crisis point
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask explicitly: 'What happens to students after their funded period ends?' and 'Are there cases of students whose funding was interrupted and how were they handled?'

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Completion rates vary 20-30 percentage points across institutions in the same field; low completion rates signal structural program problems, not just student self-selection
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Request the 10-year completion rate directly from the graduate coordinator; cross-reference with CGS data if available; below 60% should prompt specific follow-up questions

decision_factors.factor: Existence of formal recourse mechanisms for advisor relationship problems
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Programs without ombudspersons or student advocates concentrate all power in the advisor; when mentorship fails, students with no formal recourse face a choice between suffering and quitting
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'Does the program have an ombudsperson or student advocate for advisor relationship issues?' and verify it is genuinely independent from faculty

decision_factors.factor: Whether the program structures multiple mentoring relationships or relies on single-advisor model
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Single-advisor models create single points of failure; students in programs with structured thesis committees and peer mentorship have better completion and career outcomes
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether thesis committee members are actively engaged or ceremonial; ask whether there are formal peer mentorship programs; ask how co-advising is handled

decision_factors.factor: Advisor's current grant status and research activity
decision_factors.why_it_matters: An advisor whose grants have expired or whose research has stagnated cannot provide adequate career support, funding continuity, or networking opportunities
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check NSF/NIH award databases for current active grants; ask students whether the advisor has new projects starting; look at publication recency

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Underrepresented students leave STEMM at higher rates due to lack of mentorship and identity conflicts with academic culture; this is a structural gap, not individual weakness
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether the advisor has successfully mentored students from similar backgrounds; ask whether the program has formal support structures for underrepresented groups; look at demographic data for completers vs. non-completers

decision_factors.factor: Peer community quality and cohort social environment
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Isolation from peer community is a predictor of attrition; cohort social environment provides informal support during the high-attrition years 5-7
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current students whether they have regular informal contact with peers; look for evidence of peer mentoring programs or cohort events

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a high-prestige lab at a top-ranked program
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Negative mentorship patterns (credit-taking, exploitation, absence) are completely invisible in rankings and publication records; prestige provides no protection against advisor dysfunction and may make it harder to leave due to sunk cost and social signaling pressure
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who sacrificed significantly to attend a prestigious program and cannot easily walk away from reputational investment

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a 4-5 year funded PhD offer without investigating what happens after
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Most students will not finish within the funded period; the funding cliff at year 4-5 coincides with the highest-attrition phase of the program, creating simultaneous financial and academic crisis
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students on visas who cannot easily take outside employment and have limited options if stipend ends before degree completion

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying entirely on a single advisor for all mentorship
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If that relationship deteriorates — which happens commonly — there is no backup network; students without alternative mentors often face binary choices between enduring dysfunction or leaving the program entirely
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students at programs that formally or informally discourage co-advising or treat thesis committees as bureaucratic formalities

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Not confronting advisor problems directly to avoid conflict
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Direct confrontation with an advisor creates retaliation risk; but silence allows problems to compound; the correct path (ombudsperson, student advocate) is unknown to most students until they are already in crisis
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from cultures where direct challenge of authority figures is socially prohibited, and international students who fear visa status complications from program conflict

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a humanities or social science PhD over STEM
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Median time to degree is 8.4-9.5 years in humanities/social sciences versus 5-6 years in STEM; this dramatically increases financial exposure, funding gap risk, and the probability of being in the high-attrition post-year-7 phase
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students whose visa and immigration timelines are directly tied to enrollment status and program completion

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Selecting a program based on department ranking rather than advisor-specific mentorship track record
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Completion rates vary significantly within institutions by advisor; a lower-ranked program with a strong mentoring advisor may produce better outcomes than a top-ranked program with an absent or exploitative one
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-generation graduate students who lack informal networks to investigate advisor reputations and rely on visible prestige signals

failure_patterns.pattern: Evaluating advisors by publication record and grant history without investigating mentorship behavior
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Publication records and grants are publicly visible and socially legible; mentorship behavior requires active investigation through conversations that applicants don't know to initiate
failure_patterns.consequence: Student enters a lab with a star researcher who is absent, exploitative, or interpersonally volatile; advisor relationship problems become the most common cited reason for leaving without a degree
warning_signs: Unable to get contact information for current lab students during visit
Advisor only discusses research outputs and publications when asked about student development

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the guaranteed funding period as the expected completion timeline
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Offer letters state funding guarantees in concrete years; actual completion statistics are not in offer letters; students anchor on the explicit number rather than the statistical distribution
failure_patterns.consequence: Student hits year 5 with no funding and an incomplete dissertation; forced to take outside work, go into debt, or abandon the degree at the most advanced stage
warning_signs: Program provides no information about what happens to students after the funded period
All examples of 'typical' completion time given by faculty are shorter than the national field average

failure_patterns.pattern: Relying on a single advisor relationship as the sole source of mentorship
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Programs are structured around single advisors; seeking additional mentors can feel like disloyalty or distrust; students don't know they have agency to build broader networks
failure_patterns.consequence: When the advisor relationship deteriorates — through advisor departure, conflict, or dysfunction — student has no alternative support structure and faces disproportionate attrition risk
warning_signs: Program culture discourages meeting with faculty outside your advisor's lab
Thesis committee meets only at formally required intervals and is not treated as a mentorship resource

failure_patterns.pattern: Underrepresented students attributing structural mentorship gaps to personal inadequacy
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The gap between underrepresented students and peers in completion rates is structural, driven by lack of identity-affirming mentorship and cultural conflicts; but when the environment doesn't name this, students internalize failure as personal
failure_patterns.consequence: Students reduce effort, disengage from the field, or leave without completing — mistakenly concluding they are not capable rather than that the mentorship structure failed them
warning_signs: Student cannot identify any mentor who has acknowledged their multiple identities (national origin, gender, first-gen status) as relevant to their experience
Student is performing well objectively but feels increasing self-doubt about belonging

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to resolve advisor dysfunction through direct confrontation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Direct communication is the culturally default conflict resolution approach; students don't know that advisor-student power asymmetry makes direct confrontation risky rather than productive
failure_patterns.consequence: Retaliation risk: advisor becomes less supportive of dissertation progress, withholds funding extensions, or creates hostile lab environment — accelerating the crisis rather than resolving it
warning_signs: Program has no clearly communicated ombudsperson or neutral third-party process
Student is considering confronting advisor without having first identified any neutral institutional resource

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming attrition is about individual fit or academic ability rather than structural program factors
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: High attrition (25-43% of starters never finishing) is not publicized by programs; survivors attribute completion to their own qualities, reinforcing the narrative that non-completers simply weren't capable
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants don't ask about program completion rates, don't investigate funding continuity, and don't treat attrition risk as a factor in choosing between programs
warning_signs: Applicant has not asked about program completion rates during the application process
Applicant is evaluating programs purely on prestige without requesting or receiving attrition data

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you spoken with a student currently in year 4 or 5 of the specific lab you are considering joining?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant has accessed the most predictive information source about advisor behavior during the highest-risk phase of the PhD
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What did that student say about advisor availability, credit attribution, and what happens when students are struggling?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The evaluation of the advisor is based on publicly visible signals (publications, rankings) that are orthogonal to mentorship quality; the most important data is missing

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the 10-year completion rate for the specific program you are considering?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant has investigated structural program quality beyond reputation; and whether the program is transparent about attrition
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the rate above 60%? If below, has the program given a specific explanation and shown evidence of improvement?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Applicant is making a major commitment without knowing whether most students who start actually finish; this is a critical information gap

diagnostic_questions.question: What does your funding package guarantee, and what has the program told you happens to students after the guaranteed period ends?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant understands the funding cliff and has a concrete plan for the 2-3 year gap between guaranteed funding end and statistical completion
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is there documented evidence of teaching assistantships, grants, or fellowships that bridge the gap? Or is the answer vague?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Applicant is operating on an implicit assumption that they will finish within the funded period, which contradicts national median data

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the program have a formal ombudsperson or student advocate who is independent of faculty?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is institutional infrastructure to handle advisor relationship problems without requiring direct confrontation; programs without this concentrate all power in the advisor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you been told how to access this person and under what circumstances they can intervene?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the advisor relationship deteriorates, the only options are direct confrontation (retaliation risk) or leaving; this significantly increases vulnerability

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you planning to rely solely on your primary advisor for mentorship, or do you have a plan for building additional mentoring relationships?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student understands single-advisor dependency risk and has or will build a multi-mentor support structure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have specific co-advisors, engaged committee members, or peer mentors been identified? Are they already in relationship with the student?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The student is entering a single-point-of-failure structure; if the primary advisor relationship fails, there is no backup network and attrition risk is substantially higher

diagnostic_questions.question: For underrepresented students: Has any faculty member in the program explicitly acknowledged your background — national origin, gender, first-generation status — as relevant to your graduate experience?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the program and advisor have the awareness and practice of identity-affirming mentorship that the National Academies identifies as predictive of retention for underrepresented students
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Was this acknowledgment superficial (diversity statement) or substantive (specific conversation about how your background might affect your experience and how they will support you)?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The student may be entering an environment where structural mentorship gaps for underrepresented students exist and are unnamed; risk of later internalizing those gaps as personal failure is high

diagnostic_questions.question: What field are you entering, and have you looked at the median time-to-degree for that field specifically?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the student's timeline expectations are calibrated to field-specific data; humanities/social science (8.4-9.5 years) vs. STEM (5-6 years) have dramatically different financial and visa exposure profiles
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the student built a financial and visa plan that accounts for the median, not the best-case, completion timeline?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The student is likely underestimating time-to-degree based on program marketing or best-case examples, creating a future financial and immigration planning gap

industry_realities.common_belief: If you get into a top-ranked PhD program, you will almost certainly finish with a degree
industry_realities.actual_reality: Even under the most favorable conditions, no more than 75% of PhD students ever complete; at many programs the 10-year completion rate is 57-63%; attrition is structural and field-wide, not a marker of individual failure
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should investigate completion rates as a standard part of program evaluation and treat programs that cannot or will not disclose this data with skepticism

industry_realities.common_belief: A famous researcher with many publications will be a good PhD advisor
industry_realities.actual_reality: Mentorship is a learned skill, not a personality trait and not correlated with research output; negative mentorship behaviors (absence, credit-taking, exploitation, volatility) are completely invisible in a publication record and only detectable by talking to current and former students
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate advisors through direct investigation of their mentorship behavior, not through their research reputation; these are independent variables

industry_realities.common_belief: The funding period stated in a PhD offer letter is roughly how long the degree will take
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most PhD funding packages guarantee 4-5 years; median time to degree nationally is 7.3 years overall and 8.4-9.5 years in humanities/social sciences; the funding cliff at year 4-5 coincides with peak attrition
industry_realities.implication: Students should treat year 4-5 funding as the beginning of a vulnerable phase, not the end of the program, and ask explicitly about institutional support structures beyond the guaranteed period

industry_realities.common_belief: If a PhD student doesn't finish, it's because they weren't capable enough or didn't fit the field
industry_realities.actual_reality: CGS data shows that completion is most strongly predicted by financial support continuity, mentoring quality, social environment, and program structure — not individual ability; attrition is a structural outcome, not a personal one
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students should evaluate structural factors (completion rates, funding continuity, mentorship infrastructure) rather than assuming their ability will overcome structural deficiencies

industry_realities.common_belief: If you have a problem with your advisor, you should address it directly with them
industry_realities.actual_reality: Direct confrontation with an advisor in a power-asymmetric relationship creates retaliation risk; the National Academies recommends neutral third-party resources (ombudspersons, student advocates) as the appropriate first contact
industry_realities.implication: Students should identify and verify the existence of neutral institutional recourse mechanisms before they need them, not during a crisis; the absence of such mechanisms should be a program selection factor

industry_realities.common_belief: Underrepresented students who leave PhD programs do so because graduate school wasn't right for them
industry_realities.actual_reality: Underrepresented students leave STEMM at higher rates than peers partly due to lack of effective mentorship and identity conflicts with academic culture; this is a structural gap, not an individual capability or fit issue
industry_realities.implication: Underrepresented students should specifically assess whether a program and advisor have demonstrated track records of supporting students with similar backgrounds, and treat the absence of this as a structural risk factor

industry_realities.common_belief: Your primary advisor is sufficient mentorship for a PhD
industry_realities.actual_reality: National Academies research shows that single-mentor models create a single point of failure; PhD students with multiple mentoring relationships — co-advisors, engaged committee members, peer mentors, external professionals — have better outcomes
industry_realities.implication: Students should proactively build multiple mentoring relationships rather than waiting for programs to structure this; and should evaluate programs partly on whether they facilitate or discourage multi-mentor structures

industry_realities.common_belief: Most institutions formally evaluate and hold accountable advisors for mentorship quality
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most institutions do not formally evaluate advisor mentorship quality; widespread adoption of effective mentorship requires systemic shifts that have not occurred in most programs
industry_realities.implication: Students cannot rely on institutional quality control to protect them from poor advisors; self-directed investigation before joining a lab is the primary protection mechanism available

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to evaluate a potential PhD advisor
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Looks at publication count, h-index, lab prestige, and university ranking; assumes a successful researcher will be a good mentor
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats research output and mentorship quality as independent variables; investigates mentorship behavior specifically by talking to current year 4-5 students; asks about meeting frequency, attribution practices, and what happened when students struggled
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Advisor relationship problems are the most commonly cited reason for leaving a PhD without a degree; choosing based on research prestige alone leaves the highest-risk variable unexamined

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Anchors on the funding guarantee period (4-5 years) as the expected completion time; treats this as a normal program length
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows that median time to degree is 7.3 years nationally (longer in humanities); plans financially and logistically for a 2-3 year gap between funding end and actual completion; asks specifically about what happens after the funded period
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The funding cliff at year 4-5 is the peak attrition period; students who did not plan for it face simultaneous financial crisis and dissertation pressure with no institutional safety net

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes that students who don't finish weren't capable or didn't fit the field; treats own admission as evidence they will complete
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows that 25-43% of PhD starters never finish; understands completion is predicted by structural factors (funding continuity, mentorship quality, peer environment) not just ability; asks about completion rates as standard due diligence
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students who believe attrition is about individual capability don't investigate structural factors before joining a program, leaving themselves exposed to predictable and avoidable risks

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Relies entirely on the primary advisor as the source of all mentorship; views seeking other mentors as potentially disloyal or unnecessary
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Proactively builds multiple mentoring relationships — co-advisors, engaged thesis committee members, peer mentors, external professionals — before the primary relationship is tested; treats this as standard risk management
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Single-advisor dependency creates a single point of failure; when the relationship deteriorates (common), students with no alternative network face binary choices between enduring dysfunction and leaving

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Either avoids addressing the problem (letting it compound) or confronts the advisor directly (creating retaliation risk)
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Knows that neutral third-party resources (ombudspersons, student advocates) are the appropriate first contact; identifies these resources proactively before they are needed; evaluates programs partly on whether such resources exist
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Direct confrontation of an advisor creates retaliation risk in a power-asymmetric relationship; students who don't know the correct pathway default to either silence or confrontation, both of which produce worse outcomes

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Evaluating a program for underrepresented student risk
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assesses fit based on research alignment and whether the environment 'feels welcoming'; takes diversity statements at face value
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Specifically asks whether the advisor has successfully mentored students with similar backgrounds; looks for structural support programs not just statements; understands that higher late-completion rates for underrepresented students reflect structural gaps, not individual pace
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Structural mentorship gaps for underrepresented students produce predictable attrition and longer time-to-degree; students who don't investigate this specifically are more likely to internalize structural failure as personal inadequacy

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: What questions to ask during program visits
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Asks about research projects, lab equipment, course requirements, and where recent graduates got jobs
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks for the 10-year completion rate; asks what happens to students after the funded period ends; asks to speak with year 4-5 students specifically; asks whether there is an ombudsperson independent of faculty; asks for advisor-specific time-to-degree data
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The questions junior applicants ask reveal publicly visible information that program marketing already provides; the questions senior applicants ask reveal the structural factors that predict whether they will actually complete the degree
